\chapter{Take Leave}
\label{ch:fa-take-leave}
\hlchaptermodality{5}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can open a short Persian conversation, check how the other person is, and close it with khodâ hâfez.}

A four-line interaction with a beginning and an end: salâm, the wellbeing check, then khodâ hâfez from both voices; then the farewell taken apart into khodâ and hâfez, and \fa{خدا}, \fa{حافظ} and \fa{خداحافظ} read off the page.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{خدا} (khodâ)}{خدا (khodâ)}]{\fa{خدا} — the Persian half of a farewell}

\label{lesson:FA-C05-khoda}



\begin{quote}
Run the known wellbeing exchange once. The next chapter adds only the final social move: ending that interaction.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{خدا}} — \emph{khodâ} — \textbf{God}
\end{quote}

From right to left: \textbf{\fa{خ}} \emph{kh} + \textbf{\fa{د}} \emph{d} + \textbf{\fa{ا}} long \emph{â}. \emph{Read it:} the word from right to left

The short \emph{o} is learned with the word rather than written as a separate letter. Keep the back-of-the-mouth \textbf{kh} gentle; clarity matters more than force.

\begin{cousinweb}
Modern \textbf{khodâ} continues Middle Persian \emph{xwadây}, “lord.” The everyday farewell will pair this inherited Persian word with an Arabic loan. That mixed history is normal Persian vocabulary, not an exception to memorize away.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{khodâ} — God
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{خدا}} from the right edge
  \item \emph{Connect:} modern \textbf{khodâ} $\leftarrow$ Middle Persian \emph{xwadây} “lord”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter carries the final long \textbf{â}? (\textbf{\fa{ا}}.) Which vowel is heard but not written separately? (The short \emph{o}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AE\%D8\%AF\%D8\%A7}{Wiktionary: \fa{خدا}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{حافظ} (hâfez)}{حافظ (hâfez)}]{\fa{حافظ} — “guardian” or “protector”}

\label{lesson:FA-C05-hafez}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{خدا}}, then say \textbf{khodâ}

Keep it separate: this lesson adds only the second word behind the farewell.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{حافظ}} — \emph{hâfez} — \textbf{guardian, protector}
\end{quote}

\emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{ح} \fa{ا} \fa{ف} \fa{ظ}} from right to left

\textbf{\fa{ا}} carries long \textbf{â}. In contemporary Persian, final \textbf{\fa{ظ}} is pronounced \textbf{z} here, so say \emph{hâ-fez}, not an English \emph{th} sound. The short \emph{e} is part of the learned word and is normally unwritten.

\begin{cousinweb}
Arabic \textbf{ḥāfiẓ} is an active participle from the root \textbf{ḥ-f-ẓ}, “guard, preserve.” Persian borrowed the word and uses its Persian pronunciation \textbf{hâfez}. Keep the useful meaning first; the root is a memory hook.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{hâfez} — guardian, protector
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{حافظ}}
  \item \emph{Connect:} Arabic \textbf{ḥ-f-ẓ} — guard, preserve
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{hâfez} contribute to the farewell? (The idea of guarding or protecting.)

Source: \href{https://www.ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=hafiz}{American Heritage Dictionary: \emph{hafiz}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{خداحافظ} (khodâ hâfez)}{خداحافظ (khodâ hâfez)}]{\fa{خداحافظ} — goodbye}

\label{lesson:FA-C05-khodahafez}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve \textbf{khodâ} and \textbf{hâfez} separately: “God” + “guardian.” Now let them become one everyday social move.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words — put the known pieces together}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{خداحافظ}} — \emph{khodâ hâfez} — \textbf{goodbye}
\end{quote}

Persian normally writes the two spoken pieces together. Start with \textbf{\fa{خدا}}, add \textbf{\fa{حافظ}}. \emph{Read it:} the joined spelling \textbf{\fa{خداحافظ}} from the right edge

Keep the two meaning layers available underneath the complete form.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{khodâ} + \textbf{hâfez}
  \item \emph{Read it:} joined \textbf{\fa{خداحافظ}}
  \item \emph{Use:} say it only when the interaction ends
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When do you use \textbf{khodâ hâfez}? (At parting, not at the opening.)

Source: \href{https://sites.la.utexas.edu/persian\_online\_resources/vocabulary-lists/meetings-introductions/}{Persian Online: Greetings List}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{(\fa{خداحافظ}, continued)}{(خداحافظ, continued)}]{(\fa{خداحافظ}, continued) — Grammar Lens — a complete wish without a full sentence}

\label{lesson:FA-C05-khodahafez-more}



\begin{quote}
Before going on: say \textbf{\fa{خداحافظ}} again, and what it means.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — a complete wish without a full sentence}]
The expression carries the protective sense “God {[}be{]} guardian,” but everyday speakers use the whole formula simply as \textbf{goodbye}. No new verb is required for beginner production. It is a broadly polite, reliable way to end the short respectful interaction built in Chapters 1–4.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} what this lesson added to \textbf{\fa{خداحافظ}}, in one sentence
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did this lesson add to \textbf{\fa{خداحافظ}}? Say it once more, without looking.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — open, check, and close}

\label{lesson:FA-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
Without looking ahead, retrieve the expression for the beginning and the expression for the end. Do not add a new middle line.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — the complete interaction}
\begin{quote}
A: \textbf{\fa{سلام}! \fa{حال} \fa{شما} \fa{چطور} \fa{است؟}} \emph{Salâm! Hâl-e shomâ chetor ast?} B: \textbf{\fa{خوبم،} \fa{ممنون}.} \emph{Khubam, mamnun.} A: \textbf{\fa{خداحافظ}.} \emph{Khodâ hâfez.} B: \textbf{\fa{خداحافظ}.} \emph{Khodâ hâfez.}
\end{quote}

Every line is already learned. \textbf{Salâm} opens; \textbf{khodâ hâfez} closes. The same farewell works for both voices, so no pronoun, agreement ending, or new register table is hiding inside the practice.

\subsection*{Your turn — the two halves of goodbye}
Take the farewell apart without the page.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item What does \textbf{khodâ} mean? (\textbf{God.}) Where is it from? (\textbf{Inherited Persian}: Middle Persian \emph{xwadây}, \textquotedblleft{}lord.\textquotedblright{})
  \item What does \textbf{hâfez} mean? (\textbf{Guardian, protector.}) Where is it from? (\textbf{Arabic} \emph{ḥāfiẓ}, from the root \textbf{ḥ-f-ẓ}, \textquotedblleft{}guard, preserve.\textquotedblright{})
  \item The pieces picture \textquotedblleft{}God {[}be{]} guardian.\textquotedblright{} Is a verb needed to say goodbye? (\textbf{No}: the whole formula means \emph{goodbye}.)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script — the halves, then the whole}
\begin{quote}
\fa{خدا} · \fa{حافظ} · \fa{خداحافظ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{خدا}}, then \textbf{\fa{حافظ}}, then the joined \textbf{\fa{خداحافظ}}, each from the right edge
\end{itemize}

(\textbf{\fa{خ}} \emph{kh}, \textbf{\fa{د}} \emph{d}, \textbf{\fa{ا}} long \emph{â} spell \textbf{\fa{خدا}}; the final \textbf{\fa{ظ}} of \textbf{\fa{حافظ}} is said \emph{z}.)

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Choose:} meeting begins $\to$ \textbf{salâm}
  \item \emph{Choose:} interaction ends $\to$ \textbf{khodâ hâfez}
  \item \emph{Run through:} both voices once with script, once without romanization
\end{itemize}
